FISHERIES STAFF TRAINING INSTITUTE The Fisheries Staff Training Institute (FSTI), established in 1962, serves as the State's institution for capacity building and human resource development in the fisheries 84 84 sector. The Institute conducts induction and in-service training programmes for all department officers. In addition to regular departmental training programmes, the Institute also organises specialised technical training for fish farmers and fishermen on emerging technologies such as Biofloc aquaculture and freshwater ornamental fish culture. Since its inception, the Institute has trained 758 personnel and provided refresher training to 364 department officers. 12. EXTENSION AND SKILL DEVELOPMENT Extension and capacity building are integral to the sustainable development of the fisheries sector. Regular awareness programmes, exhibitions, trade fairs, fishermen grievance day meetings and fish farmers' meetings provide an effective platform for 85 85 stakeholder interaction, dissemination of best practices and resolution of field level issues. Awareness campaigns are also conducted on marine safety, hygienic fish handling, sanitation at Fishing Harbours and Fish Landing Centres and conservation of fisheries resources.

items.text: Awareness campaigns are also conducted on marine safety, hygienic fish handling, sanitation at Fishing Harbours and Fish Landing Centres and conservation of fisheries resources. To ensure the swift and effective resolution of fishermen grievances regarding welfare schemes, relief measures and regulatory issues, the Hon’ble Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu has ordered that exclusive grievance redressal meetings be conducted by regional officers in all coastal districts once in every 15 days. Accordingly, such meetings are currently being held on a fortnightly basis, thereby facilitating the speedy delivery of Government services to coastal fishermen. The Department commemorates World Ocean Day (June-8), World Fisheries Day 86 86 (November-21) and National Fish Farmers' Day (July-10) every year through awareness campaigns, exhibitions, medical camps, student competitions and extension programmes to promote sustainable fisheries and recognise the contributions of fishermen and fish farmers. Outstanding performers are honoured with awards in recognition of their achievements in fisheries development and resource conservation. 12.1 Collaboration with Fisheries Research Institutions and Industry Knowledge dissemination, technology transfer and capacity building are critical for improving fish production, enhancing productivity and promoting sustainable fisheries development. Through these collaborations, the Department promotes technology transfer, scientific resource management, innovative aquaculture practices, value addition, post -harvest management and entrepreneurship. 88 88 12.2 Skill Development Programmes for Fisher Youth and Fisherfolk The Government accords high priority to skill development as a means of enhancing employability, promoting entrepreneurship and creating sustainable livelihood opportunities for fishermen, fisherwomen and fisher youth. With financial support from the Tamil Nadu Skill Development Corporation (TNSDC), the Department implements a range of demand driven training programmes across the State. The major training programmes include: • Fisheries-based livelihood activities • Seaweed cultivation and allied activities • Open sea cage aquaculture • Fish processing • Preparation and marketing of value -added fish products 89 89 So far, 8,221 beneficiaries have undergone skill development training, of whom 6,725 beneficiaries have been assisted in undertaking livelihood activities and a total expenditure of Rs.5.33 crore has been incurred towards implementation of these training programmes.

TAMIL NADU STATE APEX FISHERIES CO-OPERATIVE FEDERATION LIMITED (TAFCOFED) TAFCOFED was registered on 6 November 1991 under the Tamil Nadu Co -operative Societies Act, 1983 and has been functioning since 19 October 1992 , with its headquarters at 92 92 Chennai. As the apex co-operative institution in the fisheries sector, it plays a pivotal role in strengthening fisheries co-operatives, implementing Government welfare schemes such as supply of sales tax exempted diesel, subsidized industrial kerosene, PMMSY scheme and promoting fisheries -based livelihood activities. At present, 1,0 80 Marine Fishermen and Fisherwomen Co-operative Societies, 2 90 Inland Fisheries Co-operative Societies and 1 1 District Fishermen Co -operative Federations are affiliated to TAFCOFED. The Director of Fisheries and Fishermen Welfare functions as the Functional Registrar of the Federation, while its day-to-day administration is carried out by an Administrator/Managing Director. TAFCOFED operates through five Project Offices located at Chennai, Nagapattinam, Ramanathapuram, Thoothukudi and Nagercoil.

Under the scheme, loans of Rs.5,000 per member are extended to groups of five members for undertaking fisheries -based livelihood activities such as fish marketing, 94 94 seaweed cultivation and fish farming, with an overall project outlay of Rs.25 .00 crore. So far, 16,185 fisherwomen organised into 3,237 Joint Liability Groups and provided loans amounting to Rs.8.09 crore. 13.3 Supply of Two -Wheelers with Ice Boxes (PMMSY scheme) To strengthen retail fish marketing and improve last -mile distribution of hygienically handled fish, TAFCOFED has been sanctioned Rs.1.59 crore for supplying 506 two -wheelers fitted with insulated ice boxes under PMMSY.

TAMIL NADU FISHERIES DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION LIMITED (TNFDC) The Tamil Nadu Fisheries Development Corporation Limited (TNFDC), established in 1974 under the Companies Act, is a State owned Public Sector Undertaking of the Government of Tamil Nadu. The Corporation is mandated to develop sustainable business models in the fisheries sector and promote commercial fisheries in the State. TNFDC plays a key role in demonstrating commercially viable fisheries enterprises, promoting entrepreneurship, generating employment and supporting value addition across the fisheries value chain. Successful business models developed by the Corporation are disseminated to fisheries entrepreneurs and start-up groups to facilitate investment and enterprise development in the sector. 98 98 The Corporation is administered by a Board of Directors , headed by a Chairman appointed by the Government. The Director of Fisheries and Fishermen Welfare functions as the Managing Director of TNFDC. The TNFDC is implementing the Government schemes such as supply of sales tax exempted diesel, subsidized industrial kerosene, PMMSY scheme , etc. 14.1. Establishment of High -Quality Handline Tuna Fishermen Fish Producer Organisation (FFPO) Clusters A Pilot scheme of "Establishment of High Quality Tuna Fishermen Fish Producer Organisation (FFPO) Clusters with Phase Change Material (PCM) Based Cold Chain Facilities" to demonstrate quality enhancement of high value handline Tuna catches by the traditional craft fishermen, with sustainability certification of handline tuna fishery to increase the international market access to substantially 101 101 increase their value realization is being implemented at a cost of Rs.1.5 0 crore with 100% assistance under PMMSY. Empowering Fisherwomen through Hygienic Dry fish production A pilot project "Empowering Fisherwomen – Revitalising Dry Fish Production Using Hygienic Solar Greenhouse Clusters" to establish high quality hygienic dry fish production clusters in Tamil Nadu, involving fisherwomen dry fish producers' organizations equipped with solar greenhouse drying facilities at an estimated cost of Rs.65.00 lakh, with the funding support from Tamil Nadu Innovation Initiatives (TANII). The project is expected to deliver high quality dry fish with green certification to enhance the value realization of dry fish production through solar energy, improved hygiene practices and market linkages. 103 103 The project aims to establish two technologically advanced solar greenhouse drying units, covering an area of 1,000 sq. ft. each in the Pazhayar and Poompuhar Fishing Harbour premises in Mayiladuthurai District , using Polycarbonate Sheets (600 GSM) with temperature and humidity control systems. Jayalalithaa Fisheries University (TNJFU), established on 19 June 2012 under the Tamil Nadu Fisheries University Act, 2012, is the State's premier institution dedicated to higher education, research and extension in fisheries and allied sciences. FUTURE ROADMAP (2026–2031) Building on the strong foundation laid through sustained investments in fisheries development, welfare, infrastructure and resource management, the Department of Fisheries and Fishermen Welfare proposes to implement a comprehensive five -year roadmap to transform Tamil Nadu into a national leader in sustainable fisheries, aquaculture and the Blue Economy. The roadmap seeks to enhance fish 149 149 production and productivity, improve the livelihoods of fishers and fish farmers, strengthen climate resilience, modernize fisheries infrastructure and promote value addition, while ensuring the long -term conservation of aquatic resources. Over the next five years, the Department will focus on the following strategic priorities: i. Sustainable Growth of Fish Production: Enhance inland, marine and coastal aquaculture production through scientific fisheries management, optimal utilization of water resources, expansion of aquaculture and mariculture, improved availability of quality fish seed, species diversification and adoption of modern production technologies. ii. Strengthening Marine and Coastal Fisheries: Promote sustainable marine 150 150 fisheries through resource conservation, sea ranching, artificial reefs, mariculture, climate -resilient coastal interventions and responsible fisheries management, while safeguarding the livelihoods of traditional fishing communities. iii. Modernisation of Fisheries Infrastructure:

items.text: Strengthening Marine and Coastal Fisheries: Promote sustainable marine 150 150 fisheries through resource conservation, sea ranching, artificial reefs, mariculture, climate -resilient coastal interventions and responsible fisheries management, while safeguarding the livelihoods of traditional fishing communities. iii. Modernisation of Fisheries Infrastructure: Develop world -class fisheries infrastructure by upgrading fishing harbours, fish landing centres, Government fish farms, cold -chain facilities, fish markets and post -harvest infrastructure to improve fish quality, reduce losses and enhance market competitiveness. iv. Welfare and Livelihood Enhancement: Further strengthen social security measures, diversify livelihood opportunities, improve skill 151 151 development, promote entrepreneurship among fishers and fisherwomen and enhance income through value addition, improved market access and co-operative development. v. Strengthening the Fisheries Value Chain: Promote processing, branding, certification, domestic marketing, export-oriented production and digital marketing platforms , to improve price realisation and enhance the competitiveness of Tamil Nadu's fisheries sector. vi. Technology, Innovation and Digital Governance: Leverage modern technologies including GIS -based resource mapping, digital service delivery, scientific monitoring systems, research partnerships and innovative aquaculture practices , to support 152 152 evidence-based planning and efficient governance. vii. Climate Resilience and Resource Conservation: Adopt ecosystem -based management approaches by promoting sustainable fishing practices, biodiversity conservation, restoration of aquatic habitats, climate -resilient infrastructure and responsible utilisation of fisheries resources. viii. Institutional Strengthening and Partnerships: Strengthen Fisheries Co- operative Societies, Fish Farmer Producer Organisations, TNFDC, TAFCOFED and other institutions while fostering collaboration with research organisations, academic institutions, the private sector and community -based organisations for accelerated sectoral growth. 153 153 19.

CONCLUSION The fisheries sector occupies a pivotal position in Tamil Nadu's economy by contributing to food and nutritional security, rural employment, export earnings and the livelihoods of millions of marine and inland fishing communities. The sector has witnessed steady progress through sustained investments in fisheries infrastructure, scientific resource management, technology adoption, conservation initiatives and comprehensive welfare measures, enabling inclusive growth and improved socio-economic outcomes for fishermen and fish farmers. Recognising the immense potential of marine fisheries, inland fisheries, aquaculture and the Blue Economy, the Government of Tamil Nadu remains committed to pursuing a balanced approach that integrates economic development with environmental sustainability. 154 154 Over the next five years, the Department will focus on enhancing fish production and productivity through scientific management of fisheries resources, expansion of inland aquaculture, mariculture and seaweed farming, promotion of value addition and export -oriented fisheries, strengthening of fisheries infrastructure, adoption of advanced technologies and digital governance and improved research, extension and capacity building. The Government will continue to accord the highest priority to the welfare, safety and livelihood security of fishermen and fish farmers by strengthening social security measures, protecting the traditional fishing rights of Tamil Nadu fishermen, enhancing climate resilience and creating sustainable livelihood opportunities, particularly for fisherwomen and fisher youth.

items.text: At present, about 4 4 35% of the State’s milk production is h andled by the organised sector, comprising cooperative and private dairies, around 15% is retained for household consumption, and the remaining 50% is handled through the unorganised sector. The cooperative dairy sector serves as a vital link between milk producers and consumers through an integrated system of procurement, processing and marketing. By assuring remunerative prices, prompt payment and a reliable market for milk, it provides dairy farmers with a stable source of income while reducing market un certainties. Equally important, it ensures that consumers have access to safe, hygienic and nutritious milk and a wide range of quality dairy products at affordable prices. The Department strengthens this value chain through scientific breeding, artificial insemination, animal health care, fodder development, balanced cattle feed, livestock insurance, credit facilitation and 5 farmer capacity building. These interventions enhance the productivity and reproductive efficiency of milch animals . Further, t he Government of Tamil Nadu is committed to transforming the dairy sector into a modern, efficient and farmer -centric enterprise through sustained investments in milk procurement, processing infrastructure, value addition, market expansion and cooperative strengt hening to enhance farmer’ s income and to improve nutritional security. 2. MILK PRODUCERS CO –OPERATIVE SOCIETIES (MPCS) The MPCS constitute the foundation of the three-tier dairy cooperative structure based on the Anand Pattern. Established at the village level, these societies serve as the primary int erface between dairy farmers and the cooperative system by procuring milk directly from producers and linking them to the organised dairy sector through the DCMPU. Originally established as Milk Supply Cooperative Societies for local milk marketing, these societies have evolved into MPCS, enabling village milk producers to market their milk through the cooperative network while availing a range of input and support services. Today, they form the backbone of Tamil Nadu ’s dairy cooperative movement and play a pivotal role in improving farmer’s incomes and rural livelihoods. 17 4.1 Structure and Functions MPCS are organised at the village level to procure milk from their members. After meeting local demand, the surplus milk is transported to Bulk Milk Coolers (BMCs), Chilling Centres or dairy plants operated by the DCMPU. All milk producers residing within the operational area of a society and owning milch animals are eligible to become members. Wherever feasible, exclusive Women ’s MPCS and Scheduled Caste MPCS a re also established to promote inclusive participation in the cooperative movement. In addition to milk procurement, the societies facilitate the supply of cattle feed, mineral mixture and other essential inputs, besides providing access to breeding, veter inary and animal health services.

Before registration, a detailed field survey is conducted by Senior Inspectors (Milk) and officials of the DCMPU to assess milk production potential, livestock population, milk routes, infrastructure, financial viabil ity and milk quality. Care is taken to ensure that the proposed society does not overlap with the operational area of an existing society. However, exclusive Women ’s and Scheduled Caste MPCS may be established in the same village wherever feasible without affecting the functioning of existing societies. After completing the statutory requirements, including submission of necessary documents by the Chief Promoter, the Deputy Registrar (Dairying) registers the society in accordance with 19 the provisions of the Tamil Nadu Cooperative Societies Act and Rules. To increase the fodder production and make available adequate green fodder to the member producers of MPCS, it is planned to cultivate green fodder varieties such as cumbu -napier, lucerne, hedge lucerne, maize, sorghum, etc in 250 acres at Salem, Coimbatore, Thanjavur and Erode to produce around 10,000 MTs annually. 49 Under the National Livestock Mission (NLM) , during the current year, 25 metric tonnes of certified sorghum fo dder seed mini -kits were distributed for covering nearly 5,000 acres. 5.2.4 Strengthening Animal Health and Emergency Veterinary Services The Department will further strengthen doorstep veterinary input services and emergency animal he althcare for milk producers under the cooperative network. These initiatives are expected to improve animal health, increase farmer confidence and strengthe n the cooperative dairy system.

items.text: 6.2.3 High Genetic Merit Heifer Calves Production Unit, Karumanthurai, Salem District This unit plays an important role in strengthening the genetic base of dairy cattle in the State. High genetic merit heifer calves with positive breeding values, born under the Rashtriya Gokul Mission – Progeny Testing Programme 63 (RGM-PTP), are procured from milk producers and scientifically reared at this unit. The heifers are inseminated using semen from proven breeding bulls to produce superior - quality bull calves. The r esulting high genetic merit bull calves are inducted into the Aavin Frozen Semen Production Station, Nilgiris for future semen production, while the heifer calves are made available to dairy farmers at cost, thereby facilitating the dissemination of superi or dairy genetics across the State. 6.2.4 Aavin Skill Development Centre, Madhavaram Recognising that skilled human resources are essential for sustainable dairy development, TCMPF established the Aavin Skill Development Centre at Madhavaram. items.text: The Centre, t ogether with the Regional Training Centres functioning under the DCMPUs, serves as the State’s principal institution for capacity building of dairy farmers, 64 64 cooperative employees and other stakeholders across the three-tier dairy cooperative system. The mission of the Centre is to improve the livelihoods of rural milk producers by promoting scientific dairy farming practices and developing skilled Artificial Insemination (AI) technicians capable of delivering quality breeding services. The Centre is equippe d with modern training infrastructure, including smart classrooms, audio - visual facilities for online and hybrid learning, residential hostel facilities for men and women, dining facilities, gymnasiums, recreational amenities and round -the-clock security, providing a conducive environment for residential training programmes. Since its establishment in 2022, the Centre has emerged as a premier institution for capacity building in the dairy cooperative sector. A total of 127 training programmes have been cond ucted, 65 benefiting 1,670 employees of TCMPF and the DCMPUs. The Centre has also generated a cumulative revenue of Rs. 46.99 lakh through its training programmes. 6.2.4.1 Regional Training Centres To strengthen human resour ce development at the grassroot level, five Regional Training Centres are functioning at Salem, Madurai, Tirunelveli, Villupuram and Vellore . items.text: 80 80 8. QUALITY ASSURANCE Quality assurance forms the cornerstone of Aavin’s operations. The TCMPF and the DCMPUs maintain rigorous quality control systems to ensure that consumers receive safe, hygienic and high-quality milk and dairy products. Milk is tested at every stage of the value chain—from procurement at MPCS, BMCs and Chilling Centres to proces sing at District Union dairies and Metro Dairies. Aavin has established modern laboratories equipped with advanced analytical testing equipment to monitor product quality and food safety. Quality testing is carried out in accordance with the standards prescribed by:  Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)  Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS)  AGMARK 81  Export Inspection Council of India (EIC) 8.1 Aavin State Central Laboratory, Madhavaram The Aavin State Central Laboratory (SCL) was established at Madhavaram in August 2022 at a project cost of Rs.8.25 crore under the National Programme for Dairy Development (NPDD). To further strengthen food safety surveillance, an Advanced Pathogen Laboratory was commissioned in July 2024 at a cost of Rs.1.88 crore. The laboratory is equipped to test milk, milk products and cattle feed for antibiotic residues, pesticide residues, aflatoxins, heavy metals, melamine, nutritional parameters, adulterants and pathogenic microorganisms. The laboratory received NABL Accreditat ion on 08.11.2025, valid up to 07.11.2029 , covering 190 testing parameters. An extension laboratory is also under establishment at a cost of Rs.2.22 crore for testing drinking water, wastewater and 81 80 8.

items.text: INTRODUCTION 1.1. Cooperation - An Instrument of Inclusive Development Cooperation is widely recognized as a driving force for inclusive, people -centered and balanced socio-economic development. The word “Cooperation” comes from the Latin word ‘co-operari’, which means ‘to work together’. The word cooperation refers to a common endeavor with a common goal especially economic growth. Individuals come together to achieve a common goal through self -help and mutual assistance. They are guided by the principle of “Each for all and all for each”. A Cooperative is a voluntary, self - governing association of individuals who unite to meet their shared economic, social and cultural needs through an enterprise they jointly own and democratically control. Established on the ideal 2 2 of “self -help through mutual help” and the equitable principle of “one member, one vote”, cooperatives consider fairness and community welfare above the mere pursuit of profit. 1.2. Tamil Nadu - Birthplace of India’s Cooperative Movement Tamil Nadu holds a place of distinction as the birthplace of the cooperative movement in India. As early as in 1904, the country's first credit cooperative society was registered at Tirur, in present- day Tiruvallur District, through the pioneering efforts of Thiru Adhi Narayanayya and Thiru P. Rajagopalachari, the first Registrar of Cooperative Societies of the erstwhile Madras Province.

items.text: Rajagopalachari, the first Registrar of Cooperative Societies of the erstwhile Madras Province. The State carries a proud legacy of several national “firsts”, which includes India's first primary agricultural cooperative credit society at Tirur, Tiruvallur District (30.08.1904) , India's first cooperative urban bank, the Big Kancheepuram cooperative urban (Town) bank 3 (08.10.1904) and India's first consumer cooperative society, the Triplicane urban cooperative society (21.08.1905). items.text: 1.3. Renewed National and Global Momentum Tamil Nadu has been at the forefront and a pioneer in the cooperative movement with a legacy of more than 122 years. The sector has 4 4 gained fresh momentum at the national level with the establishment of an exclusive Ministry for Cooperation in July 2021 by the Government of India and the launch of the National Cooperation Policy 2025. The observance of 2025 as the United Nations International Year of Cooperatives further emphasizes the global relevance of the movement in promoting sustainable and inclusive development. Today, the cooperative network in the state not only serves as the backbone of rural economy by providing the much -needed credit, agricultural inputs and marketing facilities, but also access to credit for micro enterprises and small businesses in urban areas. 1.4 ORGANISATIONAL STRUCTURE 1.4.1 Administrative Set-up The Additional Chief Secretary to Government, Cooperation, Food and Consumer Protection Department, is the Secretary of the 5 Department. The Registrar of Cooperative Societies is the Head of the Department of Cooperation. At the State Headquarters, Additional Registrars of Cooperative Societies work under the control of the Registrar of Cooperative Societies, handling subjects such as Consumer Activities, Finance and Banking, Marketing, Planning and Development, Budget and Planning, Cooperative Elections. The Joint Registrars of Cooperative Societies who are posted at the Head Office assist the Additional Registrars in subjects such as Finance and Banking, Consumer Cooperatives, Statutory, Training and Law.

By providing credit at reasonable interest rates, they help protect poor individuals from exploitation by informal moneylenders and other high-interest lending institutions. In addition to 12 12 extending financial assistance, these institutions encourage a culture of savings and investment, thereby fostering long -term financial stability among their members. These cooperative credit societies make significant contributions to both rural and urban development by supporting key sectors such as agriculture an d allied activities, infrastructure, micro, small and medium industries, and services. Tamil Nadu State Apex Cooperative Bank (TNSACB) The Tamil Nadu state apex cooperative bank (TNS AC Bank) commenced op erations in 1905 as an urban cooperative bank and was redesignated as the state apex cooperative bank in 1920. Headquartered in Chennai, the bank currently operates through a network of 16 16 51 branches and one extension counter. It is registered under the Tamil Nadu Cooperative Societies Act, 1983 and functions under the regulatory guidelines of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD). The bank holds the distinction of being the first state apex coop erative bank in India to complete 100 years of operations. As the apex institution and confederation of district (DCCBs), it plays a pivotal role in the mobilisation and disbursement of agricultural and non -agricultural credit across the state. The Tamil Nadu state apex cooperative bank mobilises funds from NABARD, NCDC and other higher financial institutions and provides financial assistance to District central cooperative banks by extending funds for Short -Term Seasonal Agricultural Operations (STSAO) loa ns, cash credit facilities for medium-term agricultural lending, and refinance support for working 17 capital loans extended to weavers’ cooperative societies. In addition, the bank, in collaboration with the District central cooperative banks, provides consortium -based financial assistance scheme to cooperative sugar mills.

items.text: The first Large Sized Multipurpose Cooperative Society in the state was established in 1958 at Sathyamangalam, Erode District. These societies procure and process several products, including Mullai honey, Oriland coffee, and Kolli Hills pepper. At present a total of 40 societies are functioning and are providing a wide range of services, including credit facilities, distribution of agricultural inputs, storage facilities, and processing units. They also undertake the procurement of forest produce, carry out activities to enhance tribal income, and distribute essential commodities under the public distribution system (PDS). During the financial year 2026 –27, these societies achieved a business turnover of Rs.157 Crore from 01.04.2026 to 31.07.2026 . A State- 27 level fed eration for Large Sized Multipurpose Cooperative Societies has been functioning since 1st November 2022 to provide necessary support and coordinate their activities across the State. Door step Banking PACCS as Business Correspondents (BCs) of Central Cooperative Banks PACCS have been engaged as Business Correspondents (BCs) of Central Cooperative Banks (CCBs) with the objective of extending banking services to rural areas and regions with limited access to formal banking facilities. items.text: 64 64 Chapter - 3 COOPERATIVE MARKETING SOCIETIES The first Agricultural Producers Cooperative Marketing Society (APCMS) in Tamil Nadu was established at Kallakurichi and commenced it operations on 26.02.1918. The APCMS in Tamil Nadu have a two-tier structure, Tamil Nadu Cooperative Marketing Federation (TANFED) at the apex level and 1 15 Agricultural Producers Cooperative Marketing Societies (APCMS) at the taluk level. The cooperative marketing societies in the State provide a platform for marketing the agricultural produce by linking the farmers with the traders and this connect paves way for price discovery, facilitate the sale of agricultural produce at remunerative prices. These societies are primarily engaged in the distribution of fertilisers and other agricultural inputs, sanction of produce pledge loans against agricultural 65 produce, processing and value addition activities and providing storage facilities at nominal rent. All these activities protect the interest of farmers and help realise better income. 3.1. Tamil Nadu Cooperative Marketing Federation (TANFED) Tamil Nadu Cooperative Marketing Federation (TANFED) was established in 1959 and is functioning through 18 Regional Offices across the State. TANFED acts as a wholesaler for fertilisers and undertakes the distribution of fertilisers and other agricultural inputs through APCMS and Primary Agricultural Cooperative Credit Societies (PACCS). Subsidised fertiliser requirement of the State is allocated by the Government of India and distributed by TANFED and TCMF to cooperative societies. 65 64 Chapter - 3 COOPERATIVE MARKETING SOCIETIES The first Agricultural Producers Cooperative Marketing Society (APCMS) in Tamil Nadu was established at Kallakurichi and commenced it operations on 26.02.1918.

In order to strengthen the seed supply chain and expand farmers’ access to high -quality seeds, cooperative societies will undertake coordinated business activities with State and National seed agencies, including Bharatiya Beej S ahakari Samiti Limited (BBSSL), for procurement and distribution of certified seeds. This collaboration will ensure reliable supply of quality seeds, promote indigenous seed production, and enhance the role of the cooperative network in achieving seed security across the State. items.text: 3.4.2. Produce Pledge Loan Cooperative marketing societies provide produce pledge loans to farmers to prevent distress sale of agricultural produce. During the current year, 50% increase over last year will be issued. During 2026 -27, up to 31.7.2026, 15412.27 MT produce pledged worth Rs. 43.43 crore. items.text: The Tamil Nadu Cooperative Union established on 04.01.1914, is the Apex Institution of the cooperative movement in the State. It has 38 District Cooperative Unions and 17 Apex Cooperative Institutions as its members. What originated as a distress -relief mechanism in the early 20th Century, the movement has grown into a massive economic driver that supports rural and agricultural growth. Today, the State has one of the largest cooperative networks in the Country, with over 24830 cooperative societies across Banking, agriculture, dairy, housing, handloom, et c., spanning across rural and urban areas. The State intervention by amending the TNCSC Act of 1983 and Rules 1988, from time to time based on the modern -day needs of the economy has made the cooperative sector register an impressive growth over the years.

Today, the State has one of the largest cooperative networks in the Country, with over 24830 cooperative societies across Banking, agriculture, dairy, housing, handloom, et c., spanning across rural and urban areas. items.text: The inclusion of cooperative banks in The Banking Regulation Act and intervention by higher financial institutions like RBI and NABARD, 138 138 also gave further impetus to the development of cooperative banking sector. Cooperatives have become an integral par t of the rural economy due to the consistent credit and input support to agriculture and allied activities with focus on sustainable growth and development. Marketing and market intervention activities by and through cooperatives have ensured fair remuneration to the farmers and right price to the consumers. Cooperative network discharges an important function of ensuring food security as it serves as a retail outlet of Universal PDS that reaches every household. The Government has identified priority initiatives to be taken up by the cooperation department with a clear focus on enhancing transparency, improving efficiency and delivery effective services by adopting latest technologies, exploring opportunities, strengthening capacities and democratising 139 institutions that cater to needs and aspirations of the farmers, SHGs, youth and vulnerable sections. The Government of Tamil Nadu is fully committed to strengthen the existing network of cooperatives spread across the length and breadth of this state and impr ove their functioning through membership drives, adoption of latest technologies and taking up new ventures for creating vibrant cooperative institutions without diluting the spirit of mutualism and self-help which is the basis of the cooperation movement. ””துதுணணைைநநலலம்ம் ஆஆக்க்ககம்ம் ததரூரூஉஉம்ம் விவிணணைைநநலலம்ம் வவேேண்ண்டிடியய எஎல்ல்லலாாம்ம் ததருரும்ம்”” Purity in Action(விவிணணைைத்த்தூதூய்ய்ணணைை) Thirukural No - 651 Meaning: Good friendships bring wealth to a man But goodness of action fulfills his every desire V. items.text: Also, create awareness on consumer laws for protecting and safeguarding the rights of consumers and provide redressal. During the period of the second World War, the rationing system was introduced by Government to overcome the shortage of food commodities and regulate the distribution of essential commodities. Over the years, the rationing system was expanded, and in 1967, the Civil Supplies Department started functioning as a separate 22 department. In 1974, a Control Order was issued and the ration card system was introduced. Through this system, essential commodities such as rice, wheat, sugar and kerosene have been distributed to the public through Fair Price Shops based on family ration cards. Tamil Nadu is the only State in India implementing a distinctive Universal Public Distribution System (UPDS) effectively through this Department. Under this system, the food requirements of all sections of society are being met without any discrimination based on economic or social status. 1.1 Department Organogram The Civil Supplies and Consumer Protection Department is headed by the Director , who is responsible for the overall administration of the Department and for the implementation, monitoring and coordination of its programmes and activities. 3 At the Headquarters, a Joint Commissioner in the cadre of District Revenue Officer assists the Director in the administration and coordination of the functions of the Department. There are two Deputy Commissioners and two Assistant Commissioners at the headquarters. At Chennai, under the direct control of Director, 19 Assistant Commissioners are heading Zonal Offices and two Deputy Commissioners are heading two Divisional offices, North Division and South Division respectively. At the district level, District Supply Officers are functioning across the State in each of the 37 Districts headed by a Deputy Collector cadre officer.

Allocation of Essential Commodities: In Tamil Nadu, essential commodities are allocated to all districts on the first day of every month. The allocation for the current month is determined based on the requirements of the respective districts, the previous month’s consumption pattern and the closing stock carried forward from the previous month. Advance movement of 60% of the allocation for the next month is undertaken by Tamil Nadu Civil Supplies Corporation Godowns to the Fair Price Shops on working days commencing from 19 the 20th of the current month. This helps prevent stockout of commodities. This arrangement enables family cardholders to collect all their essential commodities from Fair Price Shops from the first day of the month itself. Family cardholders may collect their entitled quantities of essential commodities in one or two installments, according to their preference. Consequently, requests for additional kerosene allocation are being continuously made to the Central Government. Steps are being taken to update LPG connection details in the Public Distribution System (PDS) database for family cards to ensure that kerosene is distributed only to eligible cardholders. Fair Price Shops functioning in Tamil Nadu: Under the Universal Public Distribution System in Tamil Nadu, all essential commodities are distributed through an extensive network of Fair Price Shops. These shops serve as the primary delivery mechanism for Public Distribution System and play a vital role in ensuring effective distribution of essential commodities. 31 The majority of the Fair Price Shops are operated by Cooperative Societies under the control of the Co-operation Department. The remaining shops are managed by the Tamil Nadu Civil Supplies Corporation, Women’s Self-Help Groups, and other co-operative institutions. Unlike several other States, Tamil Nadu does not permit the operation of Fair Price Shops by private agencies.

Point of Sale (PoS) device: In Tamil Nadu, under the Public Distribution System, 33,750 new PoS machines and IRIS scanners have been provided in 2024-2025 under the End-to-End computerization Phase-II Project to facilitate the distribution of essential commodities to family cardholders through fair price shops. 1.4.3. Integration of electronic weighing scales with e-PoS devices: In order to ensure that proper quantity of essential commodities is distributed to family cardholders under the Public Distribution System, the integration of electronic weighing scales with the PoS devices commenced on 05.02.2024. As of July 2026, in 38,429 Fair Price Shops the weighing scale have been integrated with e-PoS devices and essential commodities are being distributed through this system. 37 1.4.4 Public Distribution System with Biometric Authentication Any person whose name is to be included as a beneficiary under the Public Distribution System must possess a valid Aadhaar number. Biometric Authentication ensures that PDS commodities are issued only to eligible family cardholders.

Implementation of the National Food Security Act, 2013 Even before the implementation of the National Food Security Act, 2013 the Government of Tamil Nadu had been continuously implementing a Universal Public Distribution System. The National Food Security Act, 2013, was adopted in Tamil Nadu in 2016 and came into effect on November 1, 2016. For effective implementation of the Act, Priority Households have been identified in accordance with the prescribed guidelines, and their details have been uploaded in the Tamil Nadu Public Distribution System (TNPDS) Portal (www.tnpds.gov.in). Priority households (PHH) family cards are issued to eligible beneficiaries from marginalized sections, economically weaker sections, vulnerable sections including persons with 45 disabilities and transgenders. Every member is eligible for 5 kg of rice free of cost in a family holding a PHH family card and 35 kg of rice free of cost to Antyodaya Anna Yojana Family card under PHH category.

Implementation of Route Optimization System: The Government of India introduced the Route Optimization System (ROS) with the objective of reducing transportation costs and ensuring the timely movement of food grains from the godowns of the Food Corporation of India (FCI) to the godowns of the Tamil Nadu Civil Supplies Corporation (TNCSC), and subsequently from the TNCSC Godowns to Fair Price Shops (FPSs). Under this system, advanced route optimization techniques are employed to identify the most efficient transportation routes, thereby reducing fuel consumption, minimizing transportation costs, and ensuring the timely delivery of food grains to Fair Price Shops. The Route Optimization Management System has been implemented in 1,871 Fair Price Shops across 25 districts in Tamil Nadu with effect from 51 April 2024. As a result, a savings of Rs.26,54,425/- have been achieved in transportation costs.

Scheme for Charitable Institutions and Hostels (Bulk Permit) In accordance with the guidelines of the Government of India, food grains (rice and wheat) are allocated under the “Welfare Institutions and Hostels Scheme” to welfare institutions (such as leprosy homes, homes for persons with differently-abled, old age homes, and homes for destitute) and hostels for Scheduled Castes (SCs), Scheduled Tribes (STs), and Other Backward Classes (OBCs) that receive financial assistance from the Central or State governments or institutions/ hostels that are directly administered by the State or Central Government Ministries. Allocations are made from godowns of the Tamil Nadu Civil Supplies Corporation (TNCSC) based on bulk authorization orders issued by the respective District Collectors (except Chennai) and the Deputy Commissioners (City) North and South (Chennai), 14 kg of rice at the rate of Rs.1/- and 1 kg of wheat at the rate of Rs.4.15. 57 To obtain this bulk authorization, the concerned institutions/hostels must be recognized by State Government departments such as the Departments of Social Justice, Social Welfare, or Tribal Welfare and must receive financial assistance from the Central or State Governments. Furthermore, the Central Government has stipulated that no charges shall be collected from beneficiaries / inmates for the food provided.

Introduction: Tamil Nadu Civil Supplies Corporation (TNCSC) was established in the year 1972, registered under Section 25 of the Companies Act, 1956 (Section 8 of Companies Act, 2013) on 1 st April 2010 and has been functioning as a “No Loss No Profit” organization. Construction of Permanent DPCs Tamil Nadu Civil Supplies Corporation constructed a Mega Direct Purchase Centre with a capacity of procuring 200 MT per day at Panchanathikottai village, Orathanadu Taluk, in Thanjavur district. This was taken up on a pilot basis for the welfare of the farmers in that region. On the receipt of paddy at the centre the paddy is cleaned with the help of winnowing machine, weighed accurately and packed in Gunny bags by using machineries. The packed paddy is then moved to the Lorries through conveyor belt without manual intervention. The functioning of the Mega Direct Purchase Centre will be augmented by providing dryer and other facilities. 69 Emphasis is being given for establishment of permanent procurement sheds in major paddy procurement villages to strengthen the procurement infrastructure. District Administration and Regional managers have to identify suitable location for construction of Permanent DPCs. Storage sheds with specifications of approximately 60 feet × 40 feet × 15 feet, with a raised floor of one foot height and a storage capacity of around 3,000 bags is being planned to be constructed on priority basis in delta districts at an estimated cost of Rs.15 lakh. 2.4.4. items.text: Guidelines followed while appointing the Hulling Agents:  Persons or Firms who own Rice mills or who has the lease or mortgage rights on rice mills and having the daily hulling capacity of 10 MT of paddy and above alone are eligible for the appointment as Hulling Agent of the Corporation. Each Hulling Agent has to give a Security Deposit to the Corporation.  The value of Security Deposit will be assessed with reference to the holding capacity, the value of paddy will be assessed at the Minimum Support Price rate, Incentive, if any, fixed by the Government of India from time to time. 87  No interest will be paid for the Security Deposit remitted and for the bank guarantee submitted by the Hulling Agent.  Allotment of paddy to the Hulling Agents is done subject to the satisfactory previous performance of the Miller after the deposit of entire rice due from the previous allotments.  Release of paddy shall not exceed 90% of the value of the Security Deposit and Bank Guarantee deposited by the Miller at any point of time and it will be monitored by check card system.  The Hulling Agent has to deliver the “resultant rice” at the rate of outturn fixed by the Government of India from time to time. At present the Government of India have fixed outturn for Boiled rice at 68% and Raw rice at 67%.The Hulling Agent shall deliver the “resultant rice” without delay.  In case of delay, the Penalty will be imposed as below: 8786 Managers of Corporation as per the guidelines issued by TNCSC after getting prior permission from the Head Office.

Information Technology Initiatives 2.13.1. Supply Chain Management (SCM): The Tamil Nadu Civil Supplies Corporation has implemented a web-based Supply Chain Management (SCM) application to ensure efficient management and real-time monitoring of the movement of essential commodities across its supply chain. The application facilitates online monitoring of commodity receipts, storage, stock transfers, dispatch, including inventory positions at all operational, buffer and semi-covered godowns of the Corporation. Computers have been provided to all operational, buffer and semi-covered godowns to facilitate online transaction processing and inventory management. The SCM application captures all inventory transactions, ensuring accurate accounting of stock and real-time monitoring of movement of commodity 116116 throughout supply chain managed by the Corporation. The SCM application is integrated with the Point of Sale (PoS) application deployed at all Fair Price Shops through a G2G API-based integration for secure, real-time exchange and synchronization of dispatch, receipt acknowledgement, and inventory transaction data.

items.text: The SCM application is integrated with the Point of Sale (PoS) application deployed at all Fair Price Shops through a G2G API-based integration for secure, real-time exchange and synchronization of dispatch, receipt acknowledgement, and inventory transaction data. The dispatch details of essential commodities from TNCSC godowns are electronically transmitted to the PoS machines installed at Fair Price Shops, while the receipt acknowledgements captured at the Fair Price Shops are automatically synchronized through the SCM application. This integration enables end-to-end traceability of commodity movement from TNCSC godowns to Fair Price Shops, and real-time visibility of inventory across the supply chain. 117 The integrated SCM application enhances transparency, accountability, inventory management, operational efficiency, and informed decision-making by providing a centralized platform for monitoring stock availability and the movement of essential commodities across TNCSC Godowns and Fair Price Shops. 2.13.2. e-DPC Application: The Tamil Nadu Civil Supplies Corporation has implemented the e-Direct Procurement Centre (e-DPC) Digital Application to facilitate transparent, efficient, and hassle-free procurement of paddy from farmers across the State. The Online digital application has been deployed in all Direct Procurement Centres functioning in the state. Point of Procurement (PoP) devices have been provided to all DPCs to enable digital procurement operations and real- time capture of procurement data. 117116 throughout supply chain managed by the Corporation.

This integration enables end-to-end traceability of commodity movement from TNCSC godowns to Fair Price Shops, and real-time visibility of inventory across the supply chain. 117 The integrated SCM application enhances transparency, accountability, inventory management, operational efficiency, and informed decision-making by providing a centralized platform for monitoring stock availability and the movement of essential commodities across TNCSC Godowns and Fair Price Shops. 2.13.2. e-DPC Application: The Tamil Nadu Civil Supplies Corporation has implemented the e-Direct Procurement Centre (e-DPC) Digital Application to facilitate transparent, efficient, and hassle-free procurement of paddy from farmers across the State. The Online digital application has been deployed in all Direct Procurement Centres functioning in the state. Point of Procurement (PoP) devices have been provided to all DPCs to enable digital procurement operations and real- time capture of procurement data.

The vision of TNWC is to provide scientific storage with assured quality as per industry standards for the stored Agricultural Produce of Farmers, State Agriculture and Food Departments and other stakeholders. Initially, established with a share capital of Rs.10 Lakh each from Government of Tamil Nadu and Central Warehousing Corporation. It has seven regional offices headed by regional managers coordinating the Warehouse operations in that region. Each Warehouse is run by a Warehouse Manager.

Due to Scientific management and periodic monitoring, the storage loss, transit loss etc., are very minimal and it is only 0.04% during the financial year 2025-2026, as against the admissible storage loss of 0.5%. It also provides accessible, expeditious, and effective mechanisms for the redressal of consumer grievances. 143 144144 5.1 Consumer Protection Act, 2019 The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 was replaced by the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 which came into force on 20.07.2020 . The new Act replaced the old Act and provides a comprehensive legal framework for safeguarding the rights and interests of consumers. The Act has been designed to address emerging challenges such as e-commerce, product liability , misleading advertisements , and unfair trade practices . It also strengthens the consumer protection framework by promoting greater accountability and transparency in the marketplace. Under the provisions of the Act, Consumer Commissions have been established at the National, State, and District levels for the effective adjudication of consumer disputes. In addition, the Act introduces mediation as an alternate dispute resolution mechanism thereby 145 facilitating the speedy and amicable settlement of consumer disputes. 5.2 Tamil Nadu Consumer Protection Rules 2023:

District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission 6.1 National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission: The National Commission is the Apex quasi- judicial body functioning at New Delhi. It has original jurisdiction of cases dealing with complaints where the value of goods or services 162162 paid as consideration exceeds rupees two crores. The National Commission also acts as Appellate and Revisional authority over the State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions. 6.2 State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission: In the state of Tamil Nadu, the State Commission is the Apex quasi-judicial body functioning at Chennai. Any consumer can file a complaint before the State Commission, provided where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration, exceeds Fifty Lakh rupees but does not exceed two Crore rupees. The State Commission is headed by a retired Judge of High Court as the President with two Judicial Members and three Non-Judicial Members.

items.text: Vetri Thamizhagam Vision The Vetri Thamizhagam Vision envisages a paradigm shift from conventional water resources development towards integrated river basin management, sustainable utilisatio n of surface and groundwater resources, ecological restoration of rivers, climate adaptation and creation of resilient irrigation infrastructure. The Vision seeks to maximize the utilization of available water resources through scientific planning, int er-basin transfer of surplus floodwaters, modernization of irrigation systems, 2 2 groundwater recharge, flood mitigation and protection of river ecosystems. The Vision envisages fierce protection of Tamil Nadu’s rights in interstate water sharing. The Governm ent will take all necessary legal , technical and administrative steps to ensure that every drop of water due to the State reaches to the farmers and people of Tamil Nadu. ii. Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) Sustainable Development Goals are an inter-governmental set of 17 aspirational Goals with 169 targets that comes under 2030 Agenda adopted by 193 United Nations Members in 2015, further elaborated through indicators focused on measurable outcomes. NITI Aayog, with the Prime Minister as its chairperson, has been entrusted with the role to co -ordinate with States and Central Territories for SDGs. The State Planning Commission has formed working groups with various Head of Departments as members for implementation of SDGs in Tamil Nadu. Water Resources 3 3 Department is one of the members of the working groups. The Chief Engineer & Director, Institute for Water Studies, Hydrology & Quality Control has been nominated as a nodal officer for Water Resources Department. The values for the following seven indicators pertaining to Water Resources Department have been arrived and furnished for the years 2023-24 and 2024-25.

items.text: The Chief Engineer & Director, Institute for Water Studies, Hydrology & Quality Control has been nominated as a nodal officer for Water Resources Department. The values for the following seven indicators pertaining to Water Resources Department have been arrived and furnished for the years 2023-24 and 2024-25. Indicator 6.4.1 and 12.2.2 - Percentage of ground water extraction (%) against water availability: The target values for these indicators are 50%. The Percentage of ground water extraction against water availability for Tamil Nadu was 74.26% during 2023 -24 and now stands at 73.5% during the year 2024 -25. The improvement in the value indicates the improvement in availability of ground water in the St ate. Construction of Artificial Recharge Structures such as Checkdams, Bed dams, Sub surface Dykes, Recharge Shafts and Wells, 4 4 Percolation Ponds etc., contribute to this improvement. Indicator 6.4.2 - Per Capita Storage (m3/person): The target value for th is indicator is 200 m3/person per year. Tamil Nadu has surpassed the target value with a more storage of 90 Reservoirs and 14,307 Tanks under the control of Water Resources Department, 38 Reservoirs under the control of Tamil Nadu Green Energy Corporation Limited and storage structures under the control of Rural Development and Panchayat Raj Department. Due to the increase in population, the per capita storage in the state has increased from 233.99 m3/person during the year 2023 -24 to 234.62 m 3/person durin g the year 2024-25. Tamil Nadu State Water Policy Sustainable Development Goal 6 is to ensure access to water and sanitation for all. Clean and good quality water is one of the greatest challenges of 21st century. The objective of the Tamil Nadu State Water Policy is to understand the present scenario, its challenges and to propose a water policy to address the State specific concerns and challenges. The Tamil Nadu State Water Policy focus es on promoting water governance to ensure everyone's right to adequate access to water, promote economic productivity and efficient use of water resources. This policy encompasses all Government Departments, Urban and Rural Local Bodies, stakeholders and citizens of the State involved in conservation, development, harnessing, allocation, distribution and management of water resources, as well as the prevention and control of water pollution.

Water Resources Surface Water Resources The annual normal rainfall of the State is 966.70 mm. There are 34 major rivers flowing in 17 major river basins which includes 127 sub basins.The total surface water potential of the state is estimated as 865 TMC which includes rainfall in basins and water received from the neighbouring States as per Inter -State water sharing Agreements. Groundwater Resources Groundwater resources of the State also play a vital role for irrigation and drinking water needs. Therefore, to make Tamil Nadu a self - sufficient and sustainable State in ground water resources, it is the need of the hour to develop and protect the ground water resources in a more systematic manner. To conserve, collect and improve the State's groundwater, structures like Checkdams, Bed dams, sub surface dykes, water enrichment borewells, recharge wells and seepage ponds are being constructed. 12 12 The quantity and quality of ground water resources are continuously monitored and evaluated by the department. Ground Water Assessment has been completed in collaboration with Central Ground Water Board as on March 2025. The scenario of above categ orization improves based on implementation of various groundwater recharge schemes & increasing awareness on conservation of groundwater. iii. Main Activities of Water Resources Department Water is an essential natural resource for the survival of all living be ings on Earth, as well as for the growth of agriculture and industry. Tamil Nadu, having only about 3% of the country’s water resources, depends largely on South West and North East monsoon rainfall. However, uneven distribution of rainfall across regions leads to disparities in water availability. Hence, efficient water management is crucial and this responsibility is carried out by the Water Resources Department. The Water Resources Department undertakes a range of activities aimed at conservation, equitable distribution and efficient utilization of water. Its primary focus is on 14 14 conserving surface water, recharging groundwater and ensuring fair irrigation supply, particularly to tail -end areas while meeting diverse demands.

items.text: The Water Resources Department undertakes a range of activities aimed at conservation, equitable distribution and efficient utilization of water. Its primary focus is on 14 14 conserving surface water, recharging groundwater and ensuring fair irrigation supply, particularly to tail -end areas while meeting diverse demands. The Department develops irrig ation infrastructure by constructing Reservoirs, Anicuts, Barrages, Checkdams, Regulators, Canals and Channels and also rehabilitates and modernizes existing systems such as Dams, Tanks and Canals to improve efficiency. This Department engages in inter ba sin transfer and flood management measures to balance water availability and reduce damage from heavy rainfall. Monsoon water is stored and distributed for drinking and irrigation, while efforts are made to enhance storage capacity and create additional bu ffers to cope with scarcity and climate variability. Climate change challenges such as droughts, intense rainfall and floods are addressed through adaptive strategies and irrigation management is strengthened through 15 15 proper operation, maintenance and publ ic participation. In addition to that desilting and restoration programs are implemented to recover the original capacity of water bodies. Through these comprehensive measures, the Department strives to achieve water self - sufficiency, boost agricultural pr oductivity, improve livelihoods and safeguard the environment for future generations. 16 16 3. Inter State River Water Issues i. Cauvery River Water Issue Under Section 5(2) of the Inter -State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal de livered its Final Order on 05.02.2007.

items.text: 16 16 3. Inter State River Water Issues i. Cauvery River Water Issue Under Section 5(2) of the Inter -State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal de livered its Final Order on 05.02.2007. After hearing the Appeals filed by the States of Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu against the Final Order of the Tribunal, the Supreme Court delivered its Judgment on 16.02.2018 with the allocation of water as detailed below:- (in TMC) Karnataka 284.75 Tamil Nadu 404.25 Kerala 30 Pondicherry 7 Environmental Protection 10 Inevitable escapages into sea 4 Total 740 17 17 As a consequence of the aforesaid allocation, the Government of Karnataka would be required to m ake available 177.25 TMC of water to Tamil Nadu at the Inter -State border at Billigundulu. Apart from the modifications effected herein above, no interference has been made with the determination recorded by the Tribunal. As per the Judgements of the Supre me Court dated 16.02.2018 and 18.05.2018, Central Government constituted the “Cauvery Water Management Scheme, 2018”, consisting of Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA) and Cauvery Water Regulation Committee (CWRC) and notified it in its Gazette on 01.06.2018. The Government of Tamil Nadu nominated the Principal Secretary, Water Resources Department as the Member of Tamil Nadu in the Cauvery Water Management Authority and the Chief Engineer, Water Resources Department, Tiruchirappalli Region as the Me mber of Tamil Nadu in the Cauvery Water Regulation 18 18 Committee.
